Figure 39 highlights differences in wording for sentences regarding the same category. The first sentence is an example from the academic corpus, sourced from Bae et al., and the second sentence is an example from the industry corpus sourced from Gurman107. Figure 39. Excerpts from both corpora discussing the idea of policy and incentives While both sentences are discussing concepts surrounding policy, only the academic sentence explicitly uses the term while the trade journal makes a reference to policy through the related concept of regulations while also focusing on capital costs. Referring to the LDA results presented in Figure 38, we see that policy/incentives is a low saliency topic that does not surpass a score of 0.4 in the best case (academic corpus testing). Figure 37 helps us understand why the c-TF-IDF scores shown in Figure 38 for policy/incentives is much higher. This is because BERTopic can pick up on the non-literal references to a category (policy/incentives) through its synonyms (regulations), such as in the trade journal sentence. While regulation is a part of the set of synonyms in the synonym map for policy/incentives in the LDA process, the randomization experiment does not always choose it as a representative term, which demotes its assessed salience when using methods such as LDA. Because START incorporates extracted saliency from LDA as well as maintaining sentence structure importance through BERTopic, START scores can be used to formulate a clear and actionable ranking of the perception categories presented above. 107 Gurman RO. Holistic ranking of adoption perceptions MDHD EV Adoption Perception Category Rankings It should be clear that the START scores for ranking perceptions from mining topic models are somewhat volatile and open to different interpretations. The weighting scheme used to create START is also subject to change and can have an impact, as can the unequal sizes of the corpora (two topics that are left for future study). Further, volatility is to be expected when trying to model something as complex and subjective as the perceptions of human beings. With this said, the list in Figure 40 provides a firm starting point for understanding the important factors involved in MDHD EV fleet purchasing decisions. To arrive here, we mainly adhere to START scores extracted from the industry corpus but take the saliency experiments described in section 0 into consideration. Results Applied to Adoption Modeling Another benefit of the START metric of category importance is that it can be used with predefined categories of interest.
